motion: Is the physical resurrection of Jesus the best explanation for Christianity's origins?

bridges.description: Show that physical resurrection best explains Christianity's origins without claiming deductive necessity.
Establish that the Gospels and Acts preserve substantially trustworthy, close-to-events testimony.
Argue that the reported encounters resist honest mistake and that costly proclamation supports sincerity.
Argue that religious context and the purpose of signs keep resurrection from an automatically disqualifying prior probability.
Challenge resurrection's comparative superiority and favor a natural explanation of Christian origins.
Argue that oral development, literary dependence, historical kernels and elaboration can explain the texts without eyewitness authorship.
Keep a sincere-mistake origin live and question whether named witnesses' precise claims and risks are independently established.
Argue that testimony alone does not overcome the lower prior probability assigned to a miracle while allowing stronger documentation to matter.

sections.title: Burdens and competing explanations
sections.rationale: The debate turns first on whether the issue is logical necessity, mere possibility, or comparative explanatory strength.

sections.title: Sources and eyewitness proximity
sections.rationale: The central factual dispute is whether mundane textual confirmations support eyewitness testimony or ordinary developing tradition.

sections.title: Encounter detail and honest mistake
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether the claimed experiences are sufficiently detailed to exclude sincere error.

sections.title: Persecution and sincerity
sections.rationale: Costly proclamation bears on deception only if the relevant witnesses, claims and risks are adequately connected.

sections.title: Miracle priors and testimony
sections.rationale: Their final direct exchange concerns whether testimonial quantity and quality can overcome a low prior for resurrection.

moves.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
moves.claim: The resurrection is the most probable explanation of apostolic testimony, considered against honest mistake, deceit, or a combination.
moves.warrant: He proposes testing the content against mistake and the circumstances against deceit.
moves.inference: If both alternatives are unlikely, the testimony's truth is comparatively favored.
